utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone and Happy New Year. The fact is there was some confusion due to the activities in the Detention Unit. I was informed that I should get down at 8.30. However, in the meantime, at 8.00, the others went for a walk while we were locked in, and I was completely helpless because they don't have enough guards to leave one on the floor. I was unable to leave on time to get prepared to pick up my things. That was the reason. There's no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Karadzic. Now the transcript is working. Very well. There are a few matters I'd like to deal with before we begin today in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remain seated. The Chamber will take a break for ten minutes in order to change the courtroom setting. --- Break taken at 10.09 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: KDZ045

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 90305 in e-court and not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, as you know, you're testifying here today with protective measures, including a pseudonym. So without saying your name out loud, can you confirm that that's your name you can see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4089, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying in the case of the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic on the 14th of April, 2000?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand there are three corrections to make to that testimony, and I'd like to go through them with you now. First, at transcript page 2942 to 2943 you testified that you were not a member of the Bosnian army in July 1995. Now, it's correct that you were demobilised from the Territorial Defence in June 1992 after being injured, but then you were remobilised on the 5th of July, 1995, after the enclave was attacked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Second, at transcript page 2945, line 8, the transcript recorded you as saying that it was about 7.200 kilometres to the free territory to Tuzla. Now, you've clarified that it's actually around 100 kilometres from Srebrenica to Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, around 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the third correction, at transcript page 2950, line 24, you testified that there were around 2.500 to 3.000 Muslim men held on the sports field at Nova Kasaba on 13 July 1995. Now, after looking at your very first statement of the 19th of July, 1995, you stated that a more accurate estimate is around 2- to 2.500 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I believe it's more precise to put it at 2- to 2.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: With those three corrections, can you confirm that your testimony in the Krstic case was accurate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, everything I said is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the witness's Krstic testimony, 65 ter number 22710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And there are --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There are six associated exhibits I would like to tender. I'll start off with there's one that we no longer seek to tender. That's number 2902. The witness didn't confirm anything about that in his prior testimony so we don't seek to tender that. The remaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Six -- are there any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will all be admitted and given number in due course, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd now like to read a summary of the witness's prior testimony. On 11 July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, the Muslim women and children went to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. The witness testified that the men did not dare to go to Potocari because they didn't trust the Serbs. Instead, around 13- to 15.000 men and boys and some 2- to 300 women went to the village of Susnjari where they formed a large column and started moving through the woods towards Muslim-held territory. Around a third of the column was armed but the witness himself did not have a weapon. On the morning of 13 July, the column encountered heavy shelling and the witness heard Serb forces calling for their surrender over a loud speaker, assuring the Muslim men that they would be exchanged in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. The witness and around 30 men who he was with at that time decided to surrender. After the men surrendered they were taken briefly to Konjevic Polje and then to a sports field at Nova Kasaba that was full of Muslim men, some 2- to 2.500 according to the witness's revised estimate that he confirmed this morning. At least 100 Bosnian Serb soldiers were also at the sports field. About 15 to 20 minutes after the witness arrived at Nova Kasaba, General Ratko Mladic came and addressed the prisoners, after which they were ordered back onto trucks waiting on the road. The witness's truck which had 119 prisoners onboard drove towards Bratunac and then stopped near a supermarket in the village of Kravica. The witness saw at least two other trucks behind his. Throughout that night the witness heard screams, moaning, cries for help, and bursts of gun-fire. Some of the prisoners in the truck were struck with rifle-butts, while five were taken out of the truck and never returned. The prisoners received no food and only one bucket of water during this time and the conditions were so hot and stuffy that some prisoners drank their own urine. Around 2 or 3 p.m. on 14 July, the prisoners were driven to a school at Petkovci. There they were ordered to put their hands behind their heads and run into the school between two lines of Serb soldiers. As they ran into school, the prisoners were kicked, slapped, hit with rifle-butts, and forced to chant phrases such as "Long live the Serb Republic" and "Srebrenica is Serb." Once inside the school, the witness was taken to a classroom on the second floor where he saw two badly beaten men covered in blood. The witness estimated that around 200 prisoners were held in that classroom once it was full. Periodically, prisoners were taken outside and the witness could hear gun-fire. After some time, the witness was taken out into the hallway where he saw a pile of discarded clothing and identification documents. He was ordered to take off his shoes and strip to the waist but allowed to keep his vest on. His hands were then bound behind his back with string or rope and he was put into another classroom. Shortly afterwards, the witness and another group of prisoners were told to board a truck. As he ran down the stairs from the second floor of the school he saw three to four dead bodies lying at the foot of the stairs. He then climbed onto a truck that was parked with its back right up to the school. It was now dark outside. Once the truck was full of Muslim men it drove for 10 to 15 minutes and then stopped. The witness could hear heavy gun-fire and yelling, and he saw a large lit-up field that was covered with the bodies of dead prisoners who were tied up and lying face down. The witness was ordered off the truck with a group of other prisoners and told to form a row. One soldier ordered the prisoners to lie down and as they started to comply, the soldiers fired at the witness's backs and heads from close-range. The witness fell forward over the bodies of prisoners who had already been executed and tried to tuck his head in between the legs of the dead bodies. As he lay there, the witness heard bursts of fire as soldiers fired into the heads of wounded prisoners, and at one point a soldier walked over and actually kicked the witness with his boot and then said, "He's dead." After some time, another survivor who was wounded crawled over to the witness and the witness managed to free this other survivor's hands which was also tied together. Together they made their escape, climbing over a mass of dead bodies and taking cover in a large concrete canal. There, the other survivor used two rocks to cut through the rope that was still binding the witness's hands behind his back. The two survivors hid in the concrete canal until the evening of 15 July when they started moving towards Tuzla. They reached the free territory on 18 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what I would like to do now is show you four photographs and ask you to describe what is in those photographs to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 14096 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise what's shown in this photo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what it is that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: We are looking at the playground in front of that school and we see the school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to assist you, I would like to ask you to mark a few things on this photograph. First can you mark the school and put an S on it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, can you describe to the Court where the trucks were parked and where the two lines of Serb soldiers were that you ran through.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. So it was right here that the trucks were at first. Yes. And the soldiers were here. We had to get off these trucks, walking by the soldiers and entering the school here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you can just put a number 1 next to where the trucks were parked.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And a number 2 next to where the two lines of soldiers that you've drawn.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: These two here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And a number 3 next to the mark you made, describing where you entered the school.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can write your witness number, number 045, just in the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And also today's date, the 9th of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not the 10th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes. The year as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please, 2012.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could I tender that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as Exhibit P4091.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4097, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have Exhibit P00214 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise what's depicted in this photo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I certainly can recognise this. These are the classrooms that we were brought into and the hallway in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to assist you again, I would like to get you to mark a few things on this photograph. Can you mark the classrooms that you just mentioned that you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, you can just see the doors of these classrooms. So it was this classroom here, the first one, the one here then, and then the one here. You can actually just see the corner of that door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, can you mark those three classrooms with a 1, a 2, and a 3.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, can you see in this photo the place where you saw the pile of discarded clothes and identifications; and if so, can you mark that with a P?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, that place can be seen very well. It was right here by the metal railing. I'm going to mark it with a P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just one question about the identifications. At any time after you surrendered, when you were at Konjevic Polje, at Nova Kasaba, at Kravica, at the Petkovci school, did the soldiers ask you for your personal details, such as your name, your age, your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, never. No one ever asked us anything, and this was the fourth time that we were being searched and that our documents were being taken away. No one ever asked us anything or registered us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: One more thing I'd like you to mark on this photo. Where were you standing when the Serb soldiers tied your hands behind your back?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Here, right by the letter P that I placed here, so it's roughly here. There was a huge pile of documents there, IDs, health IDs as well, and also some footwear and clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, if you can put your witness number again, 045, in the bottom right-hand corner and today's date.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have now Exhibit P00216 in e-court and the second page, the clean, unmarked version of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise what's shown in this photo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise this most certainly. This is the dam in Petkovci where we were executed by the dam -- the plateau, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd again like you to mark a few things on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: First can you mark the area where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: This entire plateau was full of dead people. Do I have to mark all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can just draw a big square around the outside of the area, that might be easier.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, do you recall where it was that you were shot at; and if you do remember, can you mark that spot, or roughly that spot, with an A.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, it was roughly around here. Let's mark it with an A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And one last thing, can you see on this photo the concrete canal that you hid in? And if you can't, can you put an arrow pointing in the direction of where it is.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: The canal cannot be seen directly from this plateau, but I can draw an arrow indicating the direction in which we got out. It was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put your witness number, 045, in the bottom right-hand corner and the date.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P4099.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the last photograph I'd like to show you, Witness, is 65 ter number 2913. Do you recognise what we can see in this photo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the canal that we mentioned a moment ago, where we sought shelter later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't need you to mark anything on this photo, but if you can describe what the two features at the top of the photo are that are circled in red. The first -- the left-hand circle, the building that's there, can you describe what that is.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I think it was some sort of little house, perhaps some kind of administration building because we saw a soldier with a rifle in front of that building and we saw a machine there too. So it was a building that was there before the war. It probably had to do with the dam, perhaps securing the dam. We saw a soldier there with a rifle. We got out across this plateau and went down into this canal. He could not see us from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "we," without referring to anyone's name, can you tell us who else you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I am directly referring to the man who got out together with me, who managed to save himself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you also describe what is circled -- the right-hand circle at the top of the screen in the very top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: These are big lamps that were on throughout the night on lampposts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was tendered as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as indicated, your testimony in previous case was admitted in lieu of your examination-in-chief in this case, and now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us to clarify certain things that are unclear. I'll try to put questions that are as simple as possible and that will enable you to answer with a simple yes or no. First of all, I'd like to ask you the following. The area you are from is a group of villages and hamlets; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the name of this area and what is the name of your hamlet? If that is going to threaten your identity, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot say that because this would threaten my identity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- we'll go into private session briefly. But in the meantime, please put a pause between your answer and the accused's question so that the interpreters can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, this Territorial Defence, or rather, this group, this formation, grew into the 281st Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know. I was no longer a member at that time. That is probably what the situation was, but I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your participation in the war, has it been recognised, certified?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive certificates for privatisation and other things on the basis of your participation in the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know what happened later. Perhaps they gave it to us later after the fall. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you don't know whether you received certificates that were being given to combatants, members of the BH army, and that you don't even know their number?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: That's correct, I don't know their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many certificates did you receive? Which period of time was recognised as the period of time that you participated in the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how many months did you get a certificate, and which amount did you get for what specific participation in the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know how they handed this out. Perhaps it was recognised later, but at that point in time I was not a member. I don't know how much I received. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what do you say to this, if I say that you received this for all the months of the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I tell you that I rejoined on the 5th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the meantime, did you have anything to do with the army and this brigade? Were you in some kind of relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I personally was not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive orders from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that directly because I wasn't really involved in that kind of thing. The Territorial Defence was protecting our villages, our families, our children. That's what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as you can note in the transcript, your previous question and witness's answers were not reflected in the transcript. If necessary, in your opinion, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We were having technical problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: After demobilisation was the witness recorded as a member of that unit and did he have any kind of relationship as an administrative worker or a record-taker there. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I worked in the civilian structures and I was not the record-taker in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know what was in the transcript, but can you please confirm that you did not receive a certificate recognising your entire participation in the war or did you receive, in fact, such a certificate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I did receive a certificate of some sort, but I don't remember the period that it covered or how it was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that until the 15th of June you were a member of the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that during that time the commander of that unit was Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't recall that and I told you I don't personally know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you lived there throughout that time, and after that, was the commander Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think so, yes, but as I said I had nothing to do with him or them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Well let's see this, then. Until the 15th of June did you take part in actions conducted by this unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I never took part in any action. There were no actions carried out at the time. All we did was to provide guards around our village. We were just protecting the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, can Mr. Karadzic refer to the year as well when he's reading out dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the witness correctly and Mr. Mitchell in the examination-in-chief, the witness was a member of this unit from mid-April until mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I was wounded by a shell in my left elbow when it fell near our village, and I can prove that. I was wounded by a shrapnel from a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there any Serbs in your area, in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say you didn't participate, and while you were there you say that the unit was not carrying out any actions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I didn't participate in any personally nor do I know of any actions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D4961 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your acquaintances, Serbs, did they know that you were a member of this unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What did -- what do you mean, acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any Serb acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I did, many. When I worked together with them, many of them. And they were good friends, if I may say so, that I worked with together before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they know that you were a member of this unit and did they know your post in the unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know if they knew or not. I never had any contact with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this. These are notes to the history of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina written by people from the 28th Division unit by unit. And this is your unit here, the Territorial Defence which was used to form the 281st Light Brigade. And if you look you can see the actions carried out by that brigade. I'm just going to note the offensives. On the 1st of May, a sabotage in the sector of Zutica. Then on the 15th of May, participation in the operation of the territory between Osredak, Orahovica, Viogor, Bojna, Zeleni Jadar, with the unit in Potocari and Srebrenica. On the 16th of May, a Chetnik attack was repelled. Then on the 22nd, a successful sabotage in the sector of Zutica inflicting losses in forces and material and equipment to the enemy. And then there was an infantry attack in the sector of Bijelo Polje on the 24th of May. On the 27th, a sabotage on the enemy electricity lines. On the 29th of May, participations in fighting in Jasikovaca and Manovici. On the 3rd of June, successful sabotage in the sector of Visnjica. On the 7th of June, successful sabotage in the section of Rupovo Brdo. On the 10th of June, temporarily captured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm wondering if we can get some explanation of exactly what this document is. The second and third page have an ERN, but the first page doesn't. Perhaps there is -- Mr. Karadzic would like to give some foundation for its use before the witness answers any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But first of all, Mr. Witness, did you confirm that you belonged to 281st East Bosnian Light Brigade? Was this your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning it was the Territorial Defence. It wasn't the 281st. Later it was named the 281st Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was a bit surprised and confused by the fact that the first document you put to the witness is the one that is -- hasn't been translated, Mr. Karadzic, after such a long winter break. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Reid's checked and the first page is actually the preceding page in that ERN range but it's been -- the ERN's been cropped from it. So it does come from our collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you don't have the translation of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I didn't know that this would be disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. Can you -- were you or were you not a member of the 281st Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when it was formed later. I don't know which year. From 1995 it was the 281st, that's when I was admitted. But from mid-April, in the beginning of the war in 1992, from the 15th of June 1992, it was not actually the 281st Brigade. It was called the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do we agree that in the second paragraph it states formed from the previous unit of the Suceska TO -- rather, from the Suceska Brigade and the Lipovac Company and the Kutuzero Company from the Independent Zeleni Jadar Battalion. So the TO, a member of which you were, formed the 281st Brigade later?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're not going to move further than the 15th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear your previous answer. Was it yes, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a member of the Territorial Defence, as I said, until the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of June, successful sabotage in the sector of Rupovo Brdo. On the 10th of June, Rupovo Brdo was temporarily captured. On the 14th of June, successful sabotage against the enemy at Bijela Stijena. And then it -- I'm not going to read more because from the 15th of June this no longer refers to you. Did you know that there was so many successful sabotage actions against Serbs at the Serbian territory in your surroundings that were executed by your Territorial Defence unit, the Suceska Brigade, the Lipovac Company, and so on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know about many of them. I did hear of some but I didn't know of all of them. These are mostly Muslim villages here so it's actually the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that your unit was carrying out sabotage actions against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me. What we're talking about here is the fact that Suceska was almost entirely Muslim territory, so we're talking about defence here. But I don't know. I really cannot confirm anything either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it says here sabotage actions that were successful with losses in manpower and material and equipment on the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I had nothing to do with the command nor do I know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I completed the mining and engineering school and I also have high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I am a mining engineering technician (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D497 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Muslim society for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please let us know, Mr. Mitchell, if in your opinion any redaction is necessary. In the meantime, let us continue. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think to the second part of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Witness, we are in public session, so any testimony that may reveal your identity should be discussed in private session. Please don't hesitate to go into private session if necessary. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please not broadcast this document, 1D4947. There is a Serbian and an English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. It's time to take a break. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you heard about the international association for the union of peoples?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to them, officially or informally? Did you answer their questions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think I did, but I'm not sure when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which language did you speak to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D4947 without broadcasting, please. The Serbian version too, please. It seems the Serbian version is late. Could the witness be shown the Serbian version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we are not going to broadcast it, just hand it over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page on the ELMO. It's important because it's translated differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the translation of your conversation with that lady - I don't want to mention her name - is that right? On the first page you see the lady who spoke to you and the date this year.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't remember this name at all. I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. Could we see the Serbian version in -- on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell the Trial Chamber when you've read this, education and occupation, and if you need to see the previous occupation we can be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I want a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we go back to private session, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would like to clarify this term, to tell you what it's about. If we can go back into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a CLSS translation of the English so we'll have that looked at, that particular term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, you didn't tender the previous document, a note on the 281st East Bosnian Light Brigade. Were you minded to tender it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you. I apologise. But I didn't know the witness would contest his involvement, that's why it was not translated. But generally speaking, this entire document, the notes about the history of the -- that division would be tendered and I would like to tender this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not the witness would contest the document, the document should be translated, Mr. Karadzic. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1987, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Beginning with June 1992 until July 1992 you were not summoned into the brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I was not called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that was? There was no need; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I had been wounded and I was put back into civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you were in the civilian structures in 1993, 1994, and in 1995 until July that year. Why did they call you up only in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think it was a state of general mobilisation. Everybody had to take part. It was about defending our homes, our families, our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on 5 July 1995, the need arose for you to join the brigade. Were you then a reservist of that brigade? Were you part of the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, we were not reservists. We got involved and took part, each to the extent of their abilities, in the joint war effort. There was constant shelling and persistent attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm waiting for the interpretation and I would like you to do the same. How far was the separation line from your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Three, 4 kilometres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the Serbs across the line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: We certainly did. They had a strong howitzer, tanks, and Pragas, and they shelled us every day. My own house was shelled seven or eight times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far is your village from the centre of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about all the things and all the operations carried out by the Territorial Defence and later by the 281st Brigade in Serbian areas?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that that brigade, or rather, the Territorial Defence depending on the period, was involved in the attack against Kravica, a Serbian village, on Christmas day, 7th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I was not there. That's sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did they tell you how it happened, what happened, and how many Serbs got killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know what happened and I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war and especially after the proclamation of the protected area, what did that brigade do? By that time it was already under the command of Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know what they did. I had no insight into any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any funerals at the time? Were there any men from that brigade who got killed before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: There were people getting killed every day, civilians, including women and children, because we were shelled every day. The shells were falling all around indiscriminately. The Serb troops did not care whether they were going to kill a man, a woman, a child, or a cow. The shelling was day and night and there were civilians, simple people, getting killed every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll leave it to the observers and the Dutch Battalion to talk about that. I'm asking you about the fighting men of the 281st Brigade. In those two and a half years that the protected area existed, what were the losses of that brigade? You must have attended some funerals.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anyone from the brigade killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did they die?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot say anything with any certainty. I know only the people who got killed where I lived from shelling by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. But you were not called up before July, there was no need because the Serbs had never tried to enter the enclave on your side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: They did try many times, but I don't know the dates. I'm telling you I was part of the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us then, do you know that up until July 1995, or rather, before July 1995, the 28th Division had over 2.000 casualties among its combatants?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot confirm that, but I did hear of such figures. However, I cannot stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that almost all the combatants of the 28th Division lost their lives in Serb villages, just as Serb combatants lost their lives in Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that and I do not think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Zulfo Tursunovic was decorated with the Order of the Golden Lily?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Zulfo Tursunovic with only four years of elementary school to his name had quite a career in the military and became a celebrated commander of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I want to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said on that occasion that at first humanitarian aid arrived regularly and that it was distributed to the civilian population while the army received humanitarian aid in different ways. In which ways did the army receive humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know in which ways they received aid nor did I have any insight into their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also heard that there was some abuse of humanitarian aid, that that was talked about as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say something like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous one, 1D4943, can we have that, page 1 again. The date is the 19th of July, 1995. Can this please not be broadcast. Could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about misunderstandings between civilian and military structures, did you actually speak about this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 in Serbian and I don't know about the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the bottom. It says: "I heard -- I heard that there had been some abuse regarding the distribution, but who did that I don't know. Conflicts between the military and civilian authorities in the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. You are reading this directly and thereby disclosing my identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the question so far put to you does reveal your identity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but he's directly reading out the place that I'm from. I don't want him to disclose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be redacted if he referred to the actual hamlet where you're from, but I don't think he read out the village name. Did you read that part and could you answer the question -- what was the question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the question: Does the witness remember hearing of any abuse. And first I asked how the army received humanitarian aid because that is what the witness had stated, that they had received some aid in some way. And I asked whether there had been any abuse of humanitarian aid, and it says here, yes, that he had heard of it but he did not know who was actually involved in this and who had actually committed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim once again that I don't know who it was. Possibly there was something, but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could perhaps redact page 43, line 22, just that last word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we have to move to the main event involved because we don't have much time, Mr. Witness, but it's obvious that you had forgotten what it was that you had said at the time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I most certainly have not forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were called in the beginning of July. Were you the only person who was called up or was all of the former Territorial Defence called up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I believe that everyone was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean mobilised?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, mobilised. That's what I meant, to protect the population, to be involved in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You went to reinforce the lines there. What is the name of the area otherwise? Is it called the Bandera Triangle? You're not the only person from there. There were 5.000, 6.000 of you there, so this does not disclose your identity.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I was never in that place. We had other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that where the lines broke down first or did it happen somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think it was elsewhere, by Zeleni Jadar, that they first fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. Thank you. So you were at the front line when you heard that the lines went down and that the Serbs entered Srebrenica. When did you hear that, on which day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: The 11th, in the evening -- in the afternoon, on that Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, there was an order issued to leave the village. Who was it that issued this order to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know who ordered it, but the news arrived quickly that the entire town had fallen and that we were all supposed to leave and move towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a distinction made in that order between the civilian population and the military? What was the order issued to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think that there was no order for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it had been ordered for you to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that we had to leave, that we could not stay, that Srebrenica had fallen. It was clear that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it stated then where the civilians were supposed to go and where the soldiers were supposed to go, the able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I cannot claim that somebody had said that, but I know that all the able-bodied men, as I have already said, went into the woods, towards Susnjari, whereas the women and children went towards UNPROFOR in Potocari. They were hoping that UNPROFOR would protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did you know that your civilian authorities had accepted the fall of the enclave and that weapons were supposed to be surrendered and that everyone was supposed to act in accordance with the decision of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that. Are you referring to 1993 when demilitarisation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 11th of July, 1995, the civilian authorities came and accepted the fall of the enclave and they reached agreements with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Please explain this to me. What kind of civilian authorities? Who acceded to this? Now you have upset me. It is not true and I can never agree with what you're saying now, that someone had accepted that, that anyone from the civilian structures had accepted that. These negotiations that were conducted with Mladic were under duress and duress only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So before you left your village, did Serb soldiers enter your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, correct. A number of them in my area were already burned and then we could see that they had entered the village across and that there were bullets and shells flying and burning. It was indescribable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So which date was that? Are you trying to say that from the north-west the Serb units entered the enclave on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, on the 11th of July towards Buca and the following villages were burned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they did not enter your village when you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, were we supposed to wait to be slaughtered, just like all the others were slaughtered? Everybody was withdrawing, pulling out of the villages and we could see from a distance of 500 metres that the village was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this statement of yours that you gave to The Hague investigators -- just one moment. Let's see what number that is. In the first interview with the investigators you said that there was an order that civilians should go to Potocari and that the soldiers should go towards Jaglici and Susnjari. Is that what you stated or should we look for your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Probably it's the way I said it there. I don't know who issued the order, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the units were lined up then in Susnjari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Nobody would be able to line up 14- or 15.000 troops. It was just a question of people grouping in order for them to be able to move ahead. Simply groups were formed, a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this grouping, was that something that was done according to the brigades because there were brigades in your area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you group together with fighters of the 281st or the 282nd or the 284th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I have to say again -- can you imagine a chaotic situation, everything is burning, ammunition is flying around, and can you see in that situation how 14- or 15.000 people would make up groups? I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who commanded you from Susnjari onwards at that time, who was in command?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that there was any command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 16th of August, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 65 ter 3246, 3246, can we look at it briefly and, please, it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said on page 1 that you think that the command in Srebrenica issued the order and that in Lehovici the women separated from the men, the women and children. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could not have happened in Lehovici. I don't know how it was translated, but the separation was done on the hill in the woods above Lehovici. But in the translation it says that this was done in Lehovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what it says here in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "There was an order to go to Susnjari. The women were to go to Potocari. I believe that the order came from the Bosnian government command in Srebrenica. The women and the men walked together until we reached the village of Lehovici where we split apart." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, we separated after that village. I don't know anything about this command. I cannot really say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that there were 13- to 15.000 men there, one-third of whom were armed. Is it correct that at the front of the column were the men who were armed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't really see anyone. Probably that's how it was. I was towards the end of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that you said that one-third of them was armed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you say that the sappers were going -- walking in front of the column, going ahead of the column. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I don't recall saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there any other columns there or was this the only column that was formed in Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm anything. If you imagine a mass of 15.000 people and everyone looking to save themselves. I don't know if there were any other columns. We just all went forward en masse trying to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody there have any kind of leadership or command role?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you state that Ejub Golic took over certain duties pertaining to the column?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: All I heard after the major ambush in the night of the 12th and the 13th, that there were some 50 to 80 people who were wounded in that creek. I heard him. I didn't know him myself, I didn't see him, but I heard from people who were there that this Golic had ordered that the wounded be taken up to the hill. And I saw some 40 to 50 people definitely in the course of the night who had been seriously wounded, I saw them on the hill, Kamenicko hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know that the commander of the 281st, Zulfo Tursunovic, was in the column?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Probably he was, but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these serious attacks that were carried out against the column by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: They were serious throughout that whole period. There was shelling, howitzer fire from the area of Kravica, from the asphalt road, all along that asphalt road towards Konjevic Polje, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how was that, were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Many casualties. I just mentioned that only in the night of the 12th to the 13th I saw 40 to 50 people who were seriously wounded who were brought to that hill. I don't know what happened to those people later. I didn't hear about that from anyone, and those people were never seen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they just wounded? Nobody was killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: There were so many killed that nobody could carry them out from the creek, no one could save these people. Definitely a large number were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that nevertheless you were aware that a part of the 281st Brigade numbering about 1.000 fighters and 500 civilians, that's what the brigade comprised, and you stated that in your statement 1D4943, page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you bury the people who had -- killed in the fighting in these -- Potoci?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit of a silly question if I may say that. How could we have time to bury anyone when you don't even know what will happen to you in the next minute? We didn't even have time to look at anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who buried these people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Nobody ever did unless they were found later or the Serbs gathered them and put them in mass graves. All the rest are probably still there in those woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These are the sad consequences of civil war, but, all right, we have to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I can never agree with what you are saying, that it was a civil war. It was never a civil war. It was an attack on the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's see if you said that the brigade had 1.000 soldiers and 500 civilians. This is in the second paragraph some -- line 10 to 12 from the top. Is that correct? "We lined up in brigades and I was with our brigade, the 281st, which then had 1.000 soldiers and 500 civilians ..." And you are telling us that you had nothing to do with the brigade. But here in the statement, an early one in 1995, you said that you had lined up together with your brigade and probably all the others stood with their own brigade.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, it's been 17 or 18 years since then. I cannot recall everything that I said, but I say again, I ask you to imagine a mass of 15.000 men and how it would be possible to line them up. I'm not saying that they didn't fall into groups, but there was no proper lining up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were together with the men of the 281st Brigade, together in a group. Perhaps you did not line up, but somebody did command you on that route. It was a military breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with you. There was nobody in command. Of course we grouped together. I knew my men, my relatives, my neighbours, so we all grouped like that in the brigades. As for any kind of command, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little bit further down you say that Golic was the battalion commander and later it was said that he was Naser's deputy and that he dealt with pulling out the wounded and the dead were not taken out at all?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see anybody taking the dead out of Potok. All I saw -- and like I say, only the wounded were taken to the hill, but I did here that Golic took over. I personally did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your group, your brigade, how much did it cover? How many kilometres did it cover in the course of those two days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: If we say that we left on the 11th in the evening, up to 40 kilometres, I think, by the 13th. This was the 11th, the 12th, and the 13th in the morning. 30 -- I don't know exactly, but it's somewhere in the range of 30 to 40 kilometres on different terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And during those 40 kilometres that you covered, how much of that time were you exposed to attacks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: We have to clarify something. That section from Susnjari, some 15 or 20 kilometres, this was the free territory. So from Susnjari to Konjevic Polje -- or, rather, to Kravica, we were exposed to attacks the entire time. When we joined this route we were exposed to shelling and attacks. The biggest ambush took place on the 12th in the evening, just as it was getting dark, at about 8.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was direct combat contact, an ambush, use of fire-arms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, we were attacked. We were shelled. It was night. The shells started to fall. I don't really know exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here that those who were killed or people who were missing from your village --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just briefly move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When exactly did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think it was on the 13th in the morning -- I'm not sure, but between 11.00 and 12.00. It was a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were transported by trucks to Kravica; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Since that relative of mine - I don't want to mention his name - was badly wounded in the head, on that morning of the 13th, we were shelled in the woods all the time, and we heard them calling us to surrender all the time. And there was this white APC shuttling from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje all the time with a UN flag and that's where the voice [Realtime transcript read in error "boys"] came from, calling us to surrender, that we would all be treated by the Geneva Convention, that we should carry our dead to the -- our wounded to the road and surrender. But when we came down we were beaten by the soldiers immediately. We gave them -- we handed over our wounded and all our belongings, our ID papers, little books, whatever we had. And we were transported to Zvornik. We carried other wounded towards Konjevic Polje. I never heard what became of that relative of mine. He was found and identified in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that you saw some people committing suicide in panic, as many as 40 of them. 40 such bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I saw some incidents like that, but certainly not that many. There were 40 people lying in the creek dead or wounded. What was going on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 65 ter 3246, page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did see suicides; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No. I think I saw one, one person committing suicide, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a transcript correction at page 57, line 1, the first four words I don't think were what the witness said. So maybe that could be clarified with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How come in the transcript it's not part of the question it's part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I heard the interpreter say "that's where the voice came from."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take that to be the case. That will be corrected later on. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 4, what you said about those suicides, that they activated a grenade between them and there were dead bodies all around. It's in paragraph 1. "Two men activated a grenade, killed each other with automatic rifles. They were brothers. They shot at each other and fell to the ground. A group of four to five people took each other by the hand and -- joined hands and detonated a grenade between them. There were so many bodies and blood everywhere that every 4 or 5 metres there was another body. It was very hot and flies gathered around the bodies. The smell was terrible. I could not look at the bodies anymore. I saw about 40 bodies in total ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know that there were that many suicides. I saw that many bodies, but in the end, I heard that Serb soldiers were involved. They wore some different insignia. They engaged in wrong-doing, mixing with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said the Serb soldiers mingled with the column and did something?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes, they used tear gas and caused panic in the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know it was just a rumour and the Serb soldiers did not mix with the column? How did you allow such panic to overcome you from pure rumours?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Those were not just rumours. There were Serb soldiers within the column. We were cut off. We were the tail of the column and we were cut off from the body of the column, and I heard that there were Serb soldiers who infiltrated our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many combatants made it to Tuzla, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I never knew the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that the State Security Service, the Muslim State Security Service from Tuzla, reported that 10.000 troops from the 28th Division made it through and still more were coming?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I can tell you quite responsibly that that's not true. It never came close to that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you know if you never made it there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean I did not make it to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that 10.000 fighting men from the 28th Division made it to Tuzla and the State Security Service reports that number, saying that still more were coming. How do you know that the State Security Service did not see those men?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I'd like to see a list of those 10.000 men. I'm telling you with full responsibility that this document is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll find it in a moment. It's a report about incoming fighters. Let's go back to that moment when you were put onto several trucks. How many trucks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I was not able to count the trucks. I saw two trucks in Konjevic Polje standing and they took us to Kasaba, to the playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many people fit onto one truck?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know about the other trucks. I know only about that one truck. When Ratko Mladic addressed us in Kasaba and told his soldiers to put them back onto the truck and we arrived in Kravica, somebody said we should count ourselves. We then counted 119 on our truck. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were all taken there and remained on the truck that whole night?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: They started provoking us, interrogating us, hitting us with their rifle-butts. Those were tarp-covered trucks. People from our truck were begging for water, panic reigned on the truck. Can you imagine the heat, the temperature --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. You remained on the truck the whole night?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all the others?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: No, I believe five men were taken off the truck that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the other trucks were there and the people on them remained on board all night?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I don't know how many were taken off the other trucks, but I was able to see a little, peeping through the tarpaulin, that there were two trucks behind us and they remained there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that they were looking for specific people and you said you recognised one Grujic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could we go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your assertion that you didn't have enough time is not acceptable at all, after having spent almost an hour on trifle issues. I was struggling to understand the relevance. I was about to ask a question about that to Mr. Robinson. You have just five -- exactly five minutes. The Judges discussed it and we are not minded to extend your time at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only regret it, that this witness remains not cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were looking for a specific man, Simo. Were they looking for people in order to save them or to take their revenge on them? How did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I think they were looking for revenge, but I don't really know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the process of capturing, you say you were not listed, but they did take your ID papers away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: We took our IDs from our pockets and threw them onto a huge heap. No list was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P4098.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were those classrooms with the door just 1, 1 and a half metre away?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P4098. It doesn't have to be broadcast, although it's encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can a classroom fit there? How can this be a door leading to the classroom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I'm stating with full responsibility, and I stand by it, that those were classrooms. I don't know what the width was, I couldn't measure it, but I am asserting this is a school and those were classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
