utterances.text: Well, they would have to be 100 metres long because it's only 2 metres between the doors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue whether it's 2 or 3 metres. All I know is this is a school and these are classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the moment of the execution itself. You say you walked from the trucks. How long did you walk? How far was the execution site from the trucks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: We did not walk from the trucks. When we were brought by the trucks and when we were ordered to get off and line up again, it could have been only 5 to 10 metres away from the bodies of the people who had been brought there earlier and already killed. We did not walk anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How large were the groups, five by five? Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I seem to have heard them saying "Five men get off the truck," and then the shooting started immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of trucks were those?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: You're really asking too much. I'm trying to explain to you how afraid I was when we got there. The truck, the back of the truck was covered by the tarpaulin down to the step. But those were military trucks, a Dietz maybe was the type. It was night-time. I think that those were military trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they entered the school using that path, the track, they must have been small trucks. It couldn't have been a big truck.

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I couldn't agree. I said I don't know what kind of trucks exactly those were, what type, but I think with a 90 per cent certainty those were military trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were taken off the trucks five by five. And how long an interval could it have been between the groups? One group of five would walk 5 to 10 metres and would be executed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I'm really shattered by what I hear from you. You see all those bodies on that plateau. I myself was shot at, unconscious. I don't know how long I lay there. I don't know how long the execution lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is not against you. This is my challenging of inaccuracies and imprecisions. If it took so much time for five by five people to be executed, some things remain very unconvincing to me. There are 20 groups, five people each. How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: You are insulting me now. I'm telling you, they -- the shooting was constant. It could have lasted all night. I would be honestly ashamed to ask questions like that. A thousand people were lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There were many victims. I don't know if you were one of them. There are many contradictions and it would take a while to clear them all up. You say you saw a dam from a distance, you saw soldiers, and you saw some people from -- from the hill when you managed to get away a bit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: I did. It was not a great distance. It was only 200 metres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, now put your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you have a voluminous correspondence with the Netherlands and another country, as did the OTP on your behalf, in order to extend your stay in that country or prevent the repatriation of yourself and your numerous family members? Were many letters sent on your behalf by the OTP and you yourself to two different countries and in one of them you managed to secure residence for yourself and for your many family members --

utterances.speaker: KDZ045
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters did not hear your answer. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to ask you just about six of those reports that you wrote. You wrote three reports about the examination of Srebrenica-related remains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And there are 23 associated exhibits, 65 ter 03224 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to read a summary of Dr. Clark's evidence. In 1999 Dr. Clark oversaw the examination of human remains that were exhumed from Srebrenica-related mass graves at Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova. He describes the examination process at the mortuary and explained how his team dealt with the following four issues that were encountered during these examinations. The first issue was determining whether damage to skeletonised remains had occurred before or after death. Dr. Clark testified that where the damage was caused by gun-shot, this was generally assumed to have occurred in life as there were huge numbers of gun-shot injuries and it was not believable that all these people died in an obscure and undetected way and then were systematically shot after death. The second issue arose from the expectation that many bodies had suffered post mortem damage as a result of being piled on top of each other and compacted in graves. Dr. Clark testified that as a result of this expectation, crushing-type injuries such as fractures to the ribs and pelvis were generally interpreted as having occurred after death. He accepted that this presumption may have resulted in some genuine ante mortem blunt-force injuries being missed. The third issue was proving that damage to bone was a gun-shot injury and not something else. A gun-shot injury was only deemed to be proven where there was a typical gun-shot entrance in the bone, a typical gun-shot fragmentation pattern in a bone or where a bullet or part of a bullet was located in the body. Dr. Clark testified that as a result of relying on only these three categories the number of gun-shot injuries may well have been underestimated. The fourth issue related to the determination of cause of death in skeletonised remains. For example, where there was evidence of a gun-shot injury to the head or chest, Dr. Clark testified that it was reasonable to imply that this gun-shot was the cause of death. However, where the only evidence of gun-shot injury was to an arm or a leg, such an injury was not necessarily fatal and the cause of death would be left as unascertained. Dr. Clark then summarised his team's findings from the 1999 season as follows. From the Kozluk site, 292 bodies and 233 body parts were examined. All were male and a significant number had physical disabilities or signs of chronic disease. Blindfolds were associated with 44 bodies and ligatures with 140 bodies. Definite gun-shot injury was present in 89 per cent of those bodies. From the Nova Kasaba site, 55 bodies and two body parts were examined. The victims were all male and there were gun-shot injuries in 87 per cent of the bodies. From the Konjevic Polje site, 12 bodies were examined. One was female and the rest appeared to be male, all showed evidence of gun-shot injury. From the Glogova site, sub-graves 2 to 6, 90 bodies and 154 body parts were examined. All were male and most had been shot. There was also evidence that at least one person died from a pointed object penetrating his skull. Lastly, Dr. Clark stated that while the possibility could not be entirely excluded, there was nothing to suggest that these bodies were combat casualties. He noted the presence of blindfolds and ligatures, the fact that some bodies had significant disabilities, the patterns of gun-shot wounds to the back and single shots to the head, the absence of large numbers of wounded that would be expected in a combat situation, and the fact that nearly all of the observed injuries were caused by gun-shots when studies have shown that the most common injuries in battle are caused by shrapnel or other projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I have a few additional questions for you. In the Krstic case you testified in detail about the mortuary procedures that were in place in the 1999 season.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did those same mortuary procedures apply for 2000 and the 2001 season?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You also described the four issues or limitations on pathology evidence that were encountered in 1999. Again, were those limitations also in place in the 2000 and 2001 season?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, they applied in both these seasons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And your observations about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your observations about whether the bodies you examined in 1999 were combat casualties, again, do those observations apply to the bodies you examined in 2000 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, I have a couple of specific questions about the injuries that you observed on these bodies. In your Krstic testimony you talked about the three different categories of gun-shot injury, the clear bullet-hole, the fragmentation pattern, or the presence of a bullet or part of a bullet. Can you describe for the Court how a shrapnel injury appeared different to those three categories of gun-shot injury, in particular the gun-shot that was evidenced by a fragmentation pattern of the bone.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. A gun-shot injury of a high-velocity bullet going through bone typically causes a hole and shattering the bone round about and in a lot of cases that is what we saw. Shrapnel tends to cause much more irregular damage to a bone and perhaps over a larger area, perhaps the whole of a lower leg or a large part of the pelvis. The injuries were much more irregular. And we also based it very much on the finding not of bullet fragments but of shrapnel fragments. So we -- quite a lot of cases in which we found shrapnel and we found very irregular damage to the bone and we interpreted that as shrapnel damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And were there particular sites where you observed this shrapnel damage on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Do you mean grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. We only saw that in Glogova, one of the Glogova graves. A number in Zeleni Jadar, and there were also -- we also found shrapnel in Paklenik Cave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's Zeleni Jadar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But in none of the other sites, Kozluk, Ravnice, Lazete, no shrapnel at all in any of these sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My second question relates to something that you wrote in your 2000 Srebrenica report. I don't need to bring it up, but at page 12 of that report you talked about the devastating effect that was caused by the cavitation effect. Can you explain what the cavitation effect is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, what that means is that normally a low-power bullet will cause damage just by simply the physical hole that it produces in tissue. So it's just the physical hole of the bullet going through and if that happens to go through the heart or the brain, it causes damage just in that track. With high-velocity weapons, such as were used here, these bullets travelled at -- with tremendous amount of energy in them and when they hit something solid in the body they are slowed down greatly and they give off a tremendous amount of energy to the tissue round about. So not only do you get the physical hole where the bullet is going through but you get this huge release of energy into the tissues round about. It causes disruption of the immediate tissues round about and that is called cavitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Does cavitation also damage bones or only the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it will have the same effect on bones as on the other tissues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to take you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, now you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I'd like to ask you just a few questions about your Paklenik Cave findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can bring up the report with 65 ter number 11135. I think it was P4106. And if we can go to page 11 in both English and B/C/S, I believe. Sorry, if we can find the section in the B/C/S with the header "Cause of Death" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, can you briefly explain your findings as to the cause of death for the 73 men who you examined from this site.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we give the cause of death as listed there. The largest number, that's 27, we give the cause of death as gun-shot injury to the trunk. Then 19 as gun-shot injury to the head. Then gun-shot injuries which really covered more than one part of the body, it was in six. Gun-shot injury to the limbs was two. And head injury, which is either gun-shot that -- which really couldn't prove too much or was blunt force injury and then a small number. And then 15 was -- were unascertained, we could not determine the cause of death in these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If I can now bring up P4107, that's your supplementary report for the Paklenik Cave site. It was 65 ter 11136. Doctor, can you explain what the supplementary report is and how it relates to the findings about cause of death in the main Paklenik Cave report that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The background to this is that in the mortuary we were dealing with whole bodies -- some whole bodies. But there were also large numbers of small parts of bodies. We looked at all these in turn, but we neither had the facilities, the time, or the space to try and match up body parts to larger parts of bodies. So we might have dealt with a whole body missing the head and in a separate area there was a skull, but we really did not have the facilities to try and match these cases up. And we gave our causes of death on that basis. After our work, the bodies were handed over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, whose main work was to try and identify bodies as much as possible. They then could take quite a lot of time over these remains, and that was a specific role, and they were able to then see that that isolated skull there we think belongs to that rest of that body there. Or that lower leg there we think belongs to that. That was brought to my attention. I looked at all these in turn and went over it with them and agreed with the matching --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could stop you there for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go over to the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then, Doctor, if you could keep explaining maybe with reference to the chart that we will see on the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: So having been able to now bring a skull and associate it with the rest of the body -- and it may have been the case that the rest of the body when we looked at initially had no gun-shot injuries and we called it unascertained as the cause of death, now the skull being attached to that body, the skull with the gun-shot injury, we were able now to see that this person died from a gun-shot injury. And that's what I've tabulated in that page there, where we've associated the cases up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What about the first body part or the first body there, PK/020B --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- is that different from the other cases in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that was different and I was going to come on to that. That is something I've done myself when I was reviewing all the cases for the report. This is long since -- after the mortuary operations have finished, reviewing, going through all the files, I came across this case which was carried out by another pathologist. He had given the cause of death as unascertained. I looked at the primary evidence in his description of the report and in fact describes a bullet-hole in one of the ribs. And I've taken it upon myself to now say that that was the cause of death. It is the only case I did that for, but I thought that was justified because he actually had described the bullet-hole in the chest but for some reason had given the cause of death as unascertained. Not quite sure why he did that, but that is what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, good day. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to express my gratitude for meeting with the Defence. That was kind. And I hope that that will help us to complete this cross-examination in a pleasant manner and without any problems and I would like to thank you once again. I would like us to confirm as briefly as possible some of the things that we agreed on during the interview. Right now in front of me I have your report from 1999 of graves from Srebrenica. And on page 3 the limitations of pathological evidence. And I wanted to ask you, from the point of view of a pathologist, the main purpose of an autopsy was to examine bodies in order to establish possible injuries and where possible determine the cause of death. And then you speak about the period of time the body was in the ground and so on and so forth. Do we agree or not that other than what was said here in the first sentence, a pathologist would not be able to determine with certainty the manner of death, the time of death, the time of burial, the time that the body spent from the time of death to the time of burial, and also the distance from which shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There's a lot of questions in that. I think I could answer it by summarising that you're right that from bodies from a mass grave like this I was not able to say that these were people who died three years beforehand, four years beforehand, five years beforehand. I could tell that they had clearly been dead for some time because the bodies were decomposed, but it's difficult to be much more specific than that. They could have been -- even the bodies from the one grave could have been dead for different periods of time. That's a possibility. I'm trying to remember the other questions. They were -- yeah, the manner of death is not a phrase that I use. I always think the manner of death is for courts to decide. I determine the cause of death, whether this is gun-shot or a head injury or whatever. How that came to be I think is for other people to judge. So we talk about cause of death. We dealt with time of burial. And the last point you raise, which is slightly different but I'll answer it anyway, the distance from which shots were fired. Yes, that is very -- that was very difficult for us in decomposed bodies. The normal situation in a normal fresh body, if you like, is that we determined distance of fire because of marks, soot or flame or whatever, on the skin. Of course we have no skin or tissues in these bodies so it becomes impossible to say whether these shots were fired from 2 feet or 200 feet. I think that answers most of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. You are trying to say, isn't it right, that without soft tissue it's not possible to determine the reaction, vital reaction, to an injury and to establish whether the injury was caused before or after death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. As you will know yourself, that signs of an injury to a body are usually swelling, redness, bleeding. That indicates that something has occurred in life. That is in soft tissues. When these soft tissues are missing, then that evidence is gone. So really all we're basing our -- the examination was largely based on bones. Now, bones don't bleed, bones don't swell, bones don't go red, certainly not initially, so it -- we had -- we didn't have that advantage of the soft tissues to tell us about whether they had occurred before or after death. But I think we've probably covered that issue already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we established during the interview that you had certain information from investigators who had looked at the bodies before they reached the mortuary. And we established that you did not have sufficient information, you had the elementary facts, and would you agree that you were not informed, first of all, about the combat that lasted for 44 months and about the possibility of death in combat from April 1992 to July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that specific fact. You're correct in that we had limited information -- we were provided with limited information about the bodies in the grave. That does have its advantage in that we can look at the findings objectively and not be biased by what we think we should be finding. So some extent, really, all we knew was that these were bodies thought to be in graves, thought to be related to the Srebrenica incident. We were given little detail other than that. If it's put to me: Could all these bodies have been related to a massacre from Srebrenica at one period of time, I would say yes. Equally, if it's put to me that at least some of these bodies could have been from an earlier incident, put into the same grave, I cannot completely exclude that. Hopefully that answers that question. Just to go back to the -- you said that the investigators had seen the bodies before they reached the mortuary. I'm not sure how much -- how true that is. The investigators would have been at the grave-site, but they certainly would not have made any detailed examination of the bodies at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with that, absolutely. But you -- they saw the distribution of bodies, the grave. They were present during the investigative operations that preceded the pathologist's work, your work, in the mortuary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the investigators saw the distribution of the bodies. I'm not entirely sure what the question ... or do you think that I saw the distribution of the bodies in the -- I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Perhaps I wasn't clear. You were not present during the exhumation; that was attended by the investigators, and some of the things that they knew, they informed you about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Occasionally I did visit the exhumation site just on a -- for a brief period to see it. But I didn't look at the bodies in any great detail there and I was not given particularly detailed information by any investigators at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were thus not informed about combat continuing there for 44 months, but you were proceeding on the assumption that all the casualties were related to events from July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think that's fair, yes. I was not informed about combats prior to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your hosts didn't inform you about our legal obligations regarding the "asanacija," the clearing of terrain, after every battle. In English I think the term is "mopping-up." It's clearing the terrain from human and animal remains whereby these remains are buried in separate locations. Nobody informed you about this being one of the obligations throughout the whole war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't -- I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And nobody asked you to try to tell the difference between people who had died during the 44 months before July 1995 and those who died in July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also the casualties from July 1995, regarding those casualties you were not asked to try to establish the difference in the cause of death in terms of whether this was an execution or whether the person had been killed in battle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That question has been put to me in the courts and has been covered in previous testimonies about -- the question whether these people could have been killed in battle. In short, it is possible that some -- some of these victims could have been killed in such a situation in a battle, if by "battle" we're meaning two sets of men firing at each other with weapons, that is entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And ligatures are something that rule out that possibility and you noticed that there were people who had their hands tied or who were tied together, which would rule out the context of a battle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, this -- these were some of the factors. It's got a number of factors that would go against the idea of combat casualties. Certainly it's difficult to believe that people who had their hands tied together would be soldiers firing. We found a substantial number of people with blindfolds in a number of the grave-sites, two grave-sites in particular. So these were certainly two factors which went against a combat situation. There were others which we can go into if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that we will get to that. However, in the course of the interview you agreed that it was difficult to understand why somebody whose hands were not tied but did have a blindfold would not pull down the blindfold, why they would still keep the blindfold on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Physically it would have been possible to -- if their hands were not tied to pull the blindfold down. There may have been other pressure put on them not to do so, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your hosts inform you about the custom of Islamic fighters to wear a cotton band around their head as a symbol of their devotion to the faith and God, and we do have film footage of that and it's already been admitted. If we have time, we will try to show that, showing that many of the fighters did have such a band, ribbon, tied around their head even at the time of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That has never been put to me beforehand, before yesterday. It has to be said against that these blindfolds, I still call them blindfolds, the vast majority were still around people's eyes. They were remarkably similar from person to person, both in material, how they were tied, and in their size. And in a substantial number of them, the bullet-hole -- there were actually bullet-holes going through the blindfold, which clearly meant that -- clearly meant that they were wearing the blindfold when a shot entered the head round about the region of the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I received a correct translation, did you say a large number or a number of? From what I can remember from your findings is that the hole in the fabric did correspond to a wound in the eye and that this did not really occur too often, that there were only a few such cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that Mr. Mitchell is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Clark. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, my recollection of that footage which I believe we're talking about, the footage that was shown to Dr. Lawrence, wasn't admitted. There was a question mark over its provenance, so I'm not sure if Mr. Karadzic was mistaken or he wished to show it to this witness. But I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave it to the accused. Yes, where were we? Do you remember the question or shall I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- about to answer it. I can't remember the exact numbers, but it was probably within single figures. It was probably less than 10 or 12 that -- in which the bullet was actually through the blindfold, the bullet-hole in the blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A good part of the dilemmas, would you agree with me, while making the conclusions were the result of the restricted nature of the assumptions, assumptions that all the victims were from July 1995 and would you agree that these assumptions make it difficult to reach conclusions about the different degrees of putrefaction, degradation of the bodies, as well as other matters that the pathologists had a hard time fitting in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that there was the general assumption that these bodies all related to the same incidents. If you're putting it to me now - and it's never been put to me before - that at least some of these bodies could have been from other incidents prior to Srebrenica, that is possible. We were basing the fact that different bodies in the same grave showed different levels of decomposition on the fact that -- local factors in the grave. Perhaps one was near a much wetter part of the grave, others were more compacted together in the centre of the grave, matters like that, we -- I was thinking that was probably the explanation. And that may be true, that may be the answer. But I'm willing to accept that an alternative possibility for some of them could be that they were put in a grave at a different time or they were from a different period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And had the hosts correctly informed you about the 44 months of combat, it would have been easier for the pathologists to resolve all these dilemmas. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I would have still -- it wouldn't have solved it because I would have remained that that was a possibility but was not necessarily the true answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also agreed during the interview that you were not informed about the religious and cultural features of burial such as that the Muslims do not bury their dead in a casket but wrap them in cotton, if possible white, if not whatever is available. Because there was some cases where a body in a grave was actually wrapped in some kind of shroud, fabric. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There were -- well, it's not correct because there were not, in fact, any of the bodies from the Srebrenica sites which were wrapped in blankets or anything. You're correct that during -- in 1999 we did find bodies wrapped in blankets, but that was from the -- from Prijedor, Prijedor area, and was not in the Srebrenica sites. So there were -- none of the bodies from the Srebrenica sites were wrapped in any wrappings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, I noted that you were on foot. You wanted the reference for this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been clarified --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- I think the witness has dealt with that adequately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Unfortunately I was guided by the first notification, so I prepared all 11 reports by Dr. Clark that the Prosecution referred to -- actually, each paper that he did. So I also prepared the reports on Prijedor and Sanski Most, which now is actually superfluous. So I apologise about the confusion about the locations. I agree that this could have happened over there in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the post mortem skeletal changes, fractures, and so on, you took into account that many of those post mortem injuries and changes could have been caused because of the weight of the body, the weight of other bodies, the markings caused by machinery and so on and so forth. And if now we took as a possibility that during asanation certain graveyards were topped up rather than new ones being dug, would that digging up and filling up of graves in a subsequent asanation also contribute to fractures of older skeletons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that could apply. I mean very much we lent on the side of non-gun-shot injuries being post mortem injuries. We went that side rather than trying to interpret fractures as having occurred in life. That probably meant that we left -- that we missed some genuine fractures, but we thought it safer to err on the post mortem side. So you're correct that re-opening a grave would be one way of damaging skeletons or damaging bodies already in a grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we also agreed that in a large number of cases it was not possible to establish beyond a reasonable doubt from the point of view of a pathologist whether the death was the result of an execution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by "execution." Some people would regard execution as a person being shot from close range, typically the back of the head or the side of the head. That would be one interpretation of "execution." I would argue that a group of men at some distance away, many feet away, being shot at could equally be execution. And certainly some of the findings -- well, a lot of the findings from these grave-sites could fit with that situation. We did find a number of bodies in which the -- really the only finding was a single gun-shot injury to the back of the head. That would certainly -- was quite suggestive of a close-range shot. But as I say that I think of the situation of a group of men who are not free and who are being fired at from a distance could explain a lot of findings in a lot of the other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN 284009284 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report from 1999. I've just seen on that page that you talk about finding a large number of layers of clothing, three pairs of trousers, three coats, for example, on some of the bodies. Some -- there were some cases that in some graves there were people who were dressed in several layers of clothing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't recall it being a large number of people, but certainly there were some bodies with a remarkable amount of clothing on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your recollection - and you confirmed that in the interview - the month of July in our region is very, very hot; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your hosts also inform you of the custom to mark soldiers as protection against friendly fire with an armband or a band worn around the leg?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In almost all of your findings on some people IDs, money, valuables, watches, gold jewellery were found, whereas nothing was found on the bodies that were tied, for instance. Did you notice that distinction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It's true that we found on quite a number of people possessions as you've listed. Certainly by no means all of them and large numbers of people had no possessions. I think you're referring to the bodies that were tied as being one of the -- in the grave-site in Glogova which there were 12 men who were tied together and who had absolutely no possessions at all. Well, that was -- all I can say is that they didn't have any possessions. Some people had some possessions and who weren't in that grave and some people didn't have anything at all. I don't know what to read into that. So in other words the people -- the bodies in the Glogova grave L were not the only bodies in all of these graves to have no possessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. But we have a lot of information and we've heard a lot of testimony, especially from victims, that a person who had been previously captured would have all his identification papers and possessions taken away from them. That is customary even during peace time. In some cases, razors and lighters and watches were found. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not particularly aware of that and I don't really see it's my place to comment on that side of things. As I say, I wasn't aware that all possessions were taken away from people, but I'm willing to believe that -- if that's put to me, I'm willing to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to touch upon another topic. The question that you explained to us kindly with those ninth parts, 11 and nine-ninths [as interpreted] of the volume of the body. Would you also explain to the Trial Chamber how much of the body is taken up by one-ninth in a human?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't entirely sure what you were meaning initially, but I know now. This is something that we discussed yesterday. It was really to get -- it's how people estimate the particular size of a part of the body and it's typically used in people who've suffered burns to estimate what size of the -- what part of the body -- extent of the body has been burnt. It's called the rule of nines. It divides the body into 11 nine per cents. And it becomes a way to estimate. To go through it, the head is taken as 9 per cent. Each arm is taken as 9 per cent. The front of the trunk is taken as two nines. The back is taken as two nines. And each leg is taken as two nines. And if you total all that, it comes to 99 per cent. It's a means of estimating the extent of burning or other damage to the surface of the body. I think what you can see from that is the largest body surface is the trunk, which is from the neck to the pelvis, and then the next largest areas are the legs, in body surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. It's not only with burn victims. We could apply the same rule - and I believe you applied it - to determine the distribution of gun-shot wounds on the bodies, starting with the body, the trunk, arms and legs, and then also the side from which the shot came; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think it's fair to say that if -- if somebody -- if a person's being fired at randomly, then the greatest likelihood of what part of the body is being struck will be the trunk because it's the biggest part of the body and then after that would be the legs because, again, that's a sizeable part of the body. Now, in some of the cases that we did -- in fact, a substantial number of cases that we did, the gun-shots were fairly evenly distributed around the body in that fashion. In some grave-sites, however, it was not and that the bulk of the shots appeared to be to the trunk and there were relatively few to the legs, which goes against a sort of random distribution. So that's one observation. You talked about the direction of fire. This is -- really means the relative position of the firer and the victim. We can -- although it's quite difficult in skeletonised bodies, we can tell to some extent because when a bullet goes through a bone, the entrance side has a characteristic pattern and the exit when it comes out the other side of the body has another characteristic pattern and this is best seen in the skull. So by and large, for the majority of cases we were able to see if somebody had a gun-shot injury in the head, we could tell whether this was coming from behind them or from the side or from the front. It became more difficult to see these things in the trunk, just because of the nature of the bones, and equally it was quite difficult to see it in the limbs, the arms and the legs. From all of that and with these limitations, it has to be said that the majority of shots to these people did come from behind, particularly the head injuries, the majority were shots from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed yesterday that if one party is running away from the other, it is more likely they will be hit in the back; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you just said about the hierarchy of body parts, in Kozluk you found exactly the same, 23 per cent in the head, 37 in the trunk, then 11 per cent were hit in the legs, et cetera. Trunk, legs, head, arms, does that correspond to random fire? Does the distribution of wounds, in other words, correspond to a pattern of random fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it probably -- it would do. The head is probably over-representative -- over-represented, but the trunk and the legs would generally match random fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here in one paragraph you say that you were surprised about the legs to some extent, that there were more shot in the legs than in the head, 27 per cent compared to 23. Correct? It's the second paragraph below the table.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The direction from which the bullet came is easier to determine with the wound in the head than in other body parts; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to determine the distance from which the shot came with any certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, and I've already explained that, that it was virtually impossible for us to say whether a shot had been fired from very close range or from a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I noticed - and we discussed it yesterday during the interview - that your pathologists had difficulty explaining why there was a considerable number of bullets still in some bodies, whereas the weapons concerned had a high-velocity projectile and they were rather restricted by the assumption that all the bodies were related to July 1995 and that the bullets were fired at close range. So they concluded that perhaps the bullet had first gone through another body. If the shot came from more than 300 metres, is the likelihood the bullet would remain in the body higher than if the distance was smaller?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Again, I think there's a mixture of comments and questions there. What we found in quite a lot of the bodies was fragmented bullets, which is what you would expect if a bullet hits the body, it hits bone or something else, and breaks up. That's a normal reaction to the bullet. And we indeed found that -- these bullet fragments in a large number of people. In a smaller proportion of people, sometimes in addition to the fragments, we found a whole bullet, solid bullet, completely undamaged. Now, normally a bullet, a high-velocity bullet, if it doesn't strike bone, it will go in one side of the body and out the other undamaged. So you're right, it was a little unusual to find completely intact bullets in some of these bodies. The explanation could be that they were shot from a long distance away, a distance whereby this bullet was losing its energy and once it got into the body really didn't have the power to go much further. We're talking about hundreds of metres for that. The other possibility is that the bullet was fired from a closer range, but before it entered that victim it had lost a lot of its energy through something else and so just stayed in the body. And that could have been because it had been fired, gone through another person, perhaps through the soft tissue of another person, lost a bit of its energy, and not gone much further. It's difficult to know just why that would have occurred. It didn't have to go through another person. It could have gone through other tissues or other material perhaps and lost some of its energy there before entering that body. Just because a bullet was found with a body doesn't always mean -- did not always mean that it was always associated with that body. It may have been in the grave the bullets could move, particularly a whole body -- a whole bullet might fall from one body to another. And that's a possibility. It probably didn't occur a great deal of time, but that would be a possibility. So I don't really know the full explanation why we got intact bullets in some bodies, but there are possible explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If we now take into account this segment of the report about Kozluk concerning distribution, where distribution is consistent with random fire with many hits in the legs, most of them in the trunk but in second place are the legs, and also the numerous cases where whole bullets were still found in the body even if they had gone through another body before that which would reduce their velocity, could we exclude then the possibility that the victims got killed by fire from a distance higher than 300 metres or does that remain a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I think that that does remain a possibility. I wouldn't like to be too precise about 300 metres, it's of that order, but that would certainly have to be a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In several cases you found prior injuries. First of all, there were many fractures that were very old and completely healed and there were also injuries very close to the time of death, had been treated by immobilisation and other measures. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: If we take that in turn, you're correct that in a number of bodies that we did find old fractures, broken arms, broken legs, clearly from probably years earlier, completely healed, nothing to do with the death. As to more recent injuries, I can recall only two cases, in fact, in which we found evidence of an injury which had been bandaged and clearly -- it was a gun-shot injury, both cases were in the legs, the leg had been bandaged and splinted, which clearly indicated an injury in the days, hours, days prior to death. But I think that was only two cases and they were both from, I think, Nova Kasaba. So it certainly was not a common feature at all to find people with recent injuries, either recent healing injuries or bandaged injuries or whatever. The vast majority of people had shots which appeared to have killed them with no indication at all of injuries in the few days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In these two cases we must conclude that victims had been exposed to some kind of fire sometime before death, and in that interval somebody treated the wounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the number of those old fractures unusual for this population?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Probably not. I'm sure if you looked at any population of different ages you would find quite a lot of people who had old injuries, old fractures. So I wouldn't have thought that this was anything particularly special. We're talking about the very old injuries, the old fractures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would a fracture two or three years old qualify as old?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I would qualify an old fracture as one which is healed and the two ends of bone have come together again and the person can walk and do everything as normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the callus, which is the bone mass that heals, does not have a specific appearance and it cannot be determined whether the bone was fractured by explosion, projectile, or in another way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, just to clarify, callus refers to the healing process of a bone. If you fracture a bone in life, cells and fluid and tissues build up round about it over the following days and weeks and gradually these tissues become harder and form new bone and that's called callus and that's visible. As the process goes on further, then that disappears and all you're left with is a bone which perhaps has a slight angle to it to indicate an old fracture. So that's what callus here is. Whether that -- for an old fracture it's difficult to say what caused it, whether it was a road accident or a fall or what would be very difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But an old war injury is also not to be excluded, an injury two or three years old, without the soft tissue you cannot rule that possibility out; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: If it's an old war injury like an old bullet injury, then the fracture is likely to be much more irregular because there would be more damage to the bone. It would still be difficult to distinguish that from, say, a bad fracture caused in a road accident or other -- or some other form of accident. So it's possible that some of the quite large, old fractures could have been from war injuries, but these were not at all common.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Nova Kasaba 4, 19; 6, two; and in 7, one; and then 8, only part of a body -- actually, you've already answered that. Do you know that there was fierce fighting near Nova Kasaba. Six times or so it fell into the hands of either party. Would that have helped you, if you would know that Nova Kasaba was of special strategic importance for both sides and that there was quite a bit of fighting involved therefore?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I don't think it would have been of any difference to our findings. We just record the findings. If it was put to me that could these deaths have occurred three months beforehand for the Srebrenica, I would say yes. If it was put to me alternatively, could these all have been from -- related to the Srebrenica massacre, I would say equally, yes, they could be. So I don't think if we knew that beforehand would have made any difference in the slightest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see now the hour, Your Excellencies. Do we have to finish for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it has rather been a long day for our first day of the year. If you have more to continue, then we'll continue tomorrow morning. We'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.44 p.m.,
